name: Ethyl ascorbic acid
lead: 3-O-ethyl ascorbic acid (ethyl ascorbic acid, EAC, also written EAA or ETVC) is a vitamin C derivative used in brightening and anti-ageing skincare. People use serums and creams containing it to even out skin tone, fade dark spots and give the complexion a brighter look, since it is described as a tyrosinase inhibitor and an antioxidant [1].

Ordinary L-ascorbic acid is unstable and oxidises readily when exposed to air, and its physicochemical properties are not ideal for skin uptake; EAC was developed as a stable derivative that has been used in topical products [9]. Published work on it consists mainly of cell-culture studies, animal and porcine skin permeation studies, formulation and analytical-chemistry papers, and at least one case report of allergic contact dermatitis [2][9].

chain: Stable vitamin C ether applied to the skin
Inhibits tyrosinase and protects skin cells from UV-driven oxidative stress in lab studies
Less melanin production and a brighter, more even complexion
angle.text: EAC is a leave-on ingredient in brightening and anti-ageing products. Users apply it to lighten dark spots and even out tone, and laboratory studies describe the pathways it acts on in melanocytes and keratinocytes [1].

paras: EAC is ascorbic acid carrying an ethyl group on the 3-position of the molecule, which protects the part of the molecule that normally oxidises quickly. It is used in skincare formulations for pigment-lightening and antioxidant purposes [1]. A 2019 physicochemical characterisation described it as a stable vitamin C derivative already in use in topical products, and reported its solubility, stability, pKa and partition coefficient, along with how different neat solvents affected skin delivery [9].

Analytical methods have been published to measure it in whitening creams alongside arbutin and niacinamide, which reflects how it is commonly combined with other brightening ingredients in commercial products [3].

Products containing EAC are marketed for evening skin tone and reducing the look of hyperpigmentation. The proposed route is through melanin production: laboratory work reports that the compound inhibits tyrosinase, the enzyme at the start of the melanin pathway [1].

Because it is lipophilic and more stable than plain vitamin C, researchers have also studied it as an antioxidant for keratinocytes exposed to UV light. In vitro studies describe reduced oxidative stress and lipid peroxidation in UV-irradiated keratinocytes treated with EAC, especially when paired with cannabigerol [4][5][10][11].

A 2021 study in cultured cells reported that EAC increased the viability of UVA-irradiated keratinocytes, suppressed the ROS-mediated p53/POMC/alpha-MSH pathway, and so reduced the signals that stimulate melanocytes. Nrf2 activation and the antioxidant enzymes HO-1, gamma-GCLC and NQO-1 were involved, and silencing Nrf2 weakened the anti-melanogenic effect. In melanocytes, EAC induced autophagy and inhibited alpha-MSH-stimulated melanin synthesis [1]. The authors noted that the molecular mechanisms behind EAC had been poorly understood before that work [1].

Later in vitro studies on keratinocytes combined EAC with cannabigerol and reported lower lipid peroxidation, regulated phospholipid-metabolising enzymes, protection of membrane structure and a return of UVB-altered kinase signalling toward control levels [4][5][10][11]. Another study compared several antioxidants for protecting skin cells from UVA [6].

Much of the literature concerns getting EAC into skin. Studies describe lipid-based hydrogels and bigels that increased retention in porcine skin and showed antioxidant activity in vitro [12], lamellar liquid-crystal vehicles that improved skin retention in vitro and in vivo [8], and single-solvent systems tested for skin delivery [9]. In mouse skin, pretreatment with erbium:YAG and CO2 lasers increased permeation of EAC and another vitamin C derivative [7], and swellable microneedle patches have been explored as a way to improve transdermal delivery of acidic drugs [13].

A 2019 case report described allergic contact dermatitis caused by 3-O-ethyl ascorbic acid in facial anti-ageing cosmetics [2]. Broader safety data from systematic human studies have not been published.

No controlled clinical trials of EAC alone have been published. Research consists of in vitro cell studies, animal-skin and porcine-skin permeation work, formulation and analytical papers, and a case report of allergic contact dermatitis [1][2][7][12].

card.summary: A vitamin C ether sold for brightening; supported by lab studies, with no controlled human trials found.
card.note: At least one reported case of allergic contact dermatitis.

quick.overview:
Ethyl ascorbic acid is a modified vitamin C used in brightening serums.

Published work is mostly on cells and animal skin; no controlled human trials were found.
quick.mechanism: Lab studies report it inhibits tyrosinase and melanin production in cultured cells and has antioxidant effects in UV-exposed keratinocytes.
quick.risks: A case report documented allergic contact dermatitis from cosmetics containing it. Systematic safety data are limited.
